```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggformula)
library(ggdiagram)
library(matlib) # Matrix Functions for Teaching and Learning Linear Algebra
# pak::pak("seankross/p5")
library(p5)
##
library(symengine) # Maths Engine that does not depend upon Python!
# library(mosaicCalc) # Analytic Calculus
# library(pracma) # For numerical analysis and linear algebra
# library(Ryacas) # Symbolic Algebra

symengine_latex_matrix <- function(
  A,
  label = NULL,
  caption = NULL,
  inline = FALSE
) {
  # Accept a symengine DenseMatrix or an ordinary R matrix
  m <- if (inherits(A, "DenseMatrix")) as.matrix(A) else A

  # Ensure all entries are character strings
  m <- matrix(
    vapply(m, function(x) as.character(x), character(1)),
    nrow = nrow(m),
    ncol = ncol(m)
  )

  rows <- apply(m, 1, function(row) paste(row, collapse = " & "))

  latex_matrix <- paste0(
    "\\begin{bmatrix}\n",
    paste(rows, collapse = " \\\\\n"),
    "\n\\end{bmatrix}"
  )

  if (isTRUE(inline)) {
    return(paste0("$", latex_matrix, "$"))
  }

  # Display equation
  output <- paste0("$$\n", latex_matrix, "\n$$")

  # Optional Quarto equation label
  if (!is.null(label)) {
    output <- paste0(output, " {#", label, "}")
  }

  # Optional caption BELOW the equation
  if (!is.null(caption)) {
    output <- paste0(output, "\n\n*", caption, "*")
  }

  output
}

```


## Introduction

In this hopefully short and crisp tour, we will look at elementary operations on matrices: transpose, addition/subtraction and multiplication, and finally the inverse.

## What is a Matrix?

An rectangular array of numbers, arranged with rows and columns. A few examples are:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=48%}
@eq-3-by-3-matrix is a 3 x 3 matrix (3 rows and 3 columns).
:::
::: {.column width=48%}
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
2,3,3\\
3,1,2\\
1,2,4\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-3-by-3-matrix}
:::

::: {.column width=48%}
@eq-3-by-4-matrix is a 3 x 4 matrix (3 rows and 4 columns).
:::
::: {.column width=48%}
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
2,3,3,4\\
3,1,2,3\\
1,2,4,1\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-3-by-4-matrix}
:::

::: {.column width=48%}
@eq-1-by-4-matrix is a 1 x 4 matrix (1 rows and 4 columns).
:::
::: {.column width=48%}
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
2 ~ 3 ~ 4 ~ 2\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-1-by-4-matrix}
:::

::: {.column width=48%}
@eq-3-by-4-matrix is a 3 x 1 matrix (3 rows and 1 columns).
:::
::: {.column width=48%}
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
3\\
1\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-3-by-1-matrix}
:::
::::

## Transpose

A matrix transpose is accomplished by writing rows as columns and vice versa. Hence an $r~ \times ~ c$ matrix becomes transposed into a $c~ \times ~ r$ matrix, as shown below:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=48%}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| fig-align: center
#| 
A <- symengine::Matrix(data = c("a", "b", "c","d", "1","2"), nrow = 2, ncol = 3) 
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(A))
cat("\n\n")

```

:::

::: {.column width=4%}
:::

::: {.column width=48%}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

A <- symengine::Matrix(data = c("a", "b", "c","d", "1","2"), nrow = 2, ncol = 3) 
B <- t(A)
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(B))

```
:::

::::


## Addition and Subtraction

Matrices can be added or subtracted when they are of the ***same*** dimensions, rows and columns. Matrix elements are added or subtracted in element-wise fashion.


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=40%}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| tbl-cap: "Two Matrices"
#| 
A <- symengine::Matrix(c("a", "b", "0", "1"), 2, 2)
B <- symengine::Matrix(c("a", "b", "c", "1"), 2, 2)
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(A))
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(B))

```
:::


::: {.column width=30%}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| fig-cap: "Addition"
#| 
A <- symengine::Matrix(c("a", "b", "0", "1"), 2, 2)
B <- symengine::Matrix(c("a", "b", "c", "1"), 2, 2)
C <- A + B
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(C))

```

:::

::: {.column width=30%}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| tbl-cap: "Subtraction"
#| 
A <- symengine::Matrix(c("a", "b", "0", "1"), 2, 2)
B <- symengine::Matrix(c("a", "b", "c", "1"), 2, 2)
C <- A - B
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(C))

```

:::
::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=40%}
$$\text{Matrices A and B}$$
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{A + B}$$
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{A - B}$$
:::
::::

## Multiplication

Matrix multiplication can be visualized in many ways!! According to Gilbert Strang's famous book on Linear Algebra, there are no less than 4 very useful ways. Let us understand perhaps the easiest one, *Linear combination of Columns*.

Suppose there are three SMI peasants who bought two kinds of food and drink:

- Peasant A: 2 samosas and 1 chai
- Peasant B: 3 samosas and 0 chai
- Peasant C: 0 samosa and 2 chai-s (Just before Arvind's R class.)

Samosas cost 20 and chai costs 10. How much do they pay?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=30%}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| 
Orders <- Matrix(c(2,3,0,1,0,2),3,2) 
Prices <- Matrix(c(20, 10), 2,1) 
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(Orders))


```
:::

::: {.column width=30%}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| 
Orders <- Matrix(c(2,3,0,1,0,2),3,2) 
Prices <- Matrix(c(20, 10), 2,1) 
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(Prices))

```
:::

::: {.column width=30%}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| 
Orders <- Matrix(c(2,3,0,1,0,2),3,2) 
Prices <- Matrix(c(20, 10), 2,1) 
Bills <- Orders %*% Prices
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(Bills))
```
:::

::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{Orders}$$
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{Prices}$$
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{Bill Amounts}$$
:::
::::


We see that the first number $20$ in B multiplies the entire first column in A, and the second number $10$ multiplies the entire second column in A. These two multiplied columns are **added** to get the matrix C.

Suppose they had two options for shops? And the prices were different?

- Samosas cost 20 and chai costs 10 at Shop#1. (as before)
- Samosas cost 15 and chai costs 15 at Shop#2. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=30%}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| 
Orders <- Matrix(c(2,3,0,1,0,2),3,2) 
Menus <- Matrix(c(20, 10, 15,15), 2,2) 
Amounts <- Orders %*% Menus
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(Orders))

```

:::
::: {.column width=30%}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| 
Orders <- Matrix(c(2,3,0,1,0,2),3,2) 
Menus <- Matrix(c(20, 10, 15,15), 2,2) 
Amounts <- Orders %*% Menus
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(Menus))

```

:::
::: {.column width=30%}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
#| 
Orders <- Matrix(c(2,3,0,1,0,2),3,2) 
Menus <- Matrix(c(20, 10, 15,15), 2,2) 
Amounts <- Orders %*% Menus
cat(symengine_latex_matrix(Amounts))

```
:::
::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{Orders}$$
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{Shop Price Lists}$$
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
$$\text{Peasant Bill Options}$$
:::
::::


Shop#2 is cheaper for *Peasant#1*, and *Peasant#2*. For *Peasant#3*, Shop#1 is preferable. Drag *Peasant#3* and go to Shop#2, *Peasant#1* and *Peasant#2*.

How did this multiplication happen?

Same story as with one shop/prices, repeated to handle the second shop.
Matrix B2 now has *two* columns for prices, for Shop#1 and Shop#2.
Multiplication takes each column in B2 and does the same weighted-column-addition with A2. Hence two columns of answers in C2.

::: callout-important
### Matrix Multiplication in 4 ways
As shown in Gilbert Strang's book, there are 4 ways of thinking about matrix multiplication:

- Our method of weighting *columns* in A using *columns* B and adding
- Weighting *rows* in B using *rows* in A and adding
- Multiplying *individual values* from *rows* in A and *columns* in B and adding up, for each location in C. ( This is the common textbook method)
- Multiplying rows in A and columns in B. ( A *vectorized* version of the previous method).

For now, this one method should suffice. 
:::
